chapters.title: Welcome — A Free Gallery of Masterpieces
chapters.intro: You are standing in the nation's living room for painting. Everything here is free, almost everything is a masterpiece, and the route ahead runs in time order — gold-ground saints first, Van Gogh's sunflowers last. Take it slowly, choose a few pictures in each room, and let the building do the chronology for you.

subchapters.title: A Collection That Belongs to Everyone
subchapters.text: Here's the astonishing thing: this collection belongs, quite literally, to the British public. The National Gallery began in 1824 when the government bought 38 paintings from the banker John Julius Angerstein for £60,000 and decided the nation's art should sit in central London, where working people could see it, rather than in a royal palace out of town. Look for Hogarth's Marriage A-la-Mode among those founding pictures later on our route — it was here on day one. From those 38, the holdings have grown to over 2,300 paintings, more than 1,000 usually on display, covering Western European painting from about 1250 to 1900. No ticket and no turnstile guard them. That democratic founding idea still shapes your visit: you can walk in for twenty minutes, look at one great painting properly, and leave — and Londoners do exactly that.
subchapters.directions: Enter via the Sainsbury Wing entrance on the Trafalgar Square corner — the main entrance since its 2025 reopening — and head up to the main gallery floor.
subchapters.caption: Marriage A-la-Mode: The Marriage Settlement — William Hogarth

subchapters.title: The Building and the Sainsbury Wing
subchapters.text: Look back at the building before you climb. The porticoed block by William Wilkins opened in 1838, deliberately modest in depth — critics joked it was a pepper-pot squeezed onto the square. To the west, across a small gap, the Sainsbury Wing of 1991 by Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown echoes Wilkins in modern dress and now forms the main entrance after its Selldorf Architects remodelling, reopened in May 2025. Inside, its stone arches deliberately feel like a Renaissance church, which suits the altarpieces it holds. The whole collection hangs essentially on one main floor in four wings around a central hall, running roughly chronologically, so if you ever feel lost, ask yourself what century you want — earlier means west, later means east.
subchapters.caption: The Sainsbury Wing, National Gallery, London

subchapters.title: How to Look in This Gallery
subchapters.text: A practical word before the gold starts glowing: this gallery rewards choosing. Trying to see 1,000 paintings produces only tired eyes and a blur of Madonnas, so our route names the essential picture in each room, then the quieter neighbour most people walk past. Stand back first for the whole composition, then step close — safely behind the line — for brushwork, inscriptions and the small still-life details these painters loved hiding. Paintings are lent and moved between rooms, so if a favourite is not where you expect, ask a gallery assistant; they track every picture's current hiding place and are famously helpful about it.
subchapters.caption: Inside the National Gallery, London

subchapters.title: Trafalgar Square Outside the Door
subchapters.text: Pause on the steps and take in Trafalgar Square, laid out in the 1840s to commemorate Nelson's victory at Trafalgar in 1805. Nelson himself looks down from his 52-metre column, guarded by Edwin Landseer's four bronze lions, cast — tradition says — partly from captured French cannon. The square's fountains, added later, were partly meant to discourage huge unruly gatherings, though Londoners have ignored that intention cheerfully ever since. This is the right overture: the gallery behind you was founded in the same confident, public-spirited decades, and many of its sea pictures, portraits and histories only make full sense with this imperial, naval London just outside the door.
subchapters.caption: Nelson's Column, Trafalgar Square

subchapters.title: The Route Ahead
subchapters.text: Our walk follows the gallery's own logic. We start in the Sainsbury Wing with medieval panels made to glow by candlelight, watch perspective being invented in Florence, meet van Eyck's mirror and Botticelli's sleeping Mars, then cross into the High Renaissance of Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael. Venice and the North follow — Titian's colour, Holbein's skull, Rubens, Caravaggio and Velázquez — before Dutch quiet, British satire and landscape, and finally Monet, Seurat and Van Gogh. It is roughly two hours at a looking pace. If your energy fades, cut to the Central Hall and rejoin further east; the chronology will catch you up automatically.
subchapters.caption: Dome of the entrance hall, National Gallery, London

chapters.caption: The National Gallery from Trafalgar Square — free, and full of masterpieces

chapters.title: The Oldest Paintings — Gold, Saints and the Wilton Diptych
chapters.intro: The first rooms hold painting before painting became a window onto the world. These panels were working religious objects — altarpieces and private devotional images — made to shimmer in dim churches. Give your eyes a minute to adjust to the gold, then look for the stories pressed into it.

subchapters.title: Gold Grounds and Altarpieces
subchapters.text: That gold is not background decoration; it is theology. Gold leaf, beaten thin, laid over a red clay bole and burnished, stood for the unchanging light of heaven, a place outside ordinary time and weather — which is why saints in these panels cast no shadows and stand on patterned gold rather than earth. Most of these works began life as altarpieces above altars, seen from below by candlelight, their frames part of the architecture. When you find punch marks and tooled haloes, look closely: goldsmith techniques and painting were still one craft world. Duccio's small Annunciation panels, from the great Maestraz altarpiece for Siena Cathedral around 1308–11, show how refined this world already was before perspective arrived.
subchapters.caption: The Annunciation — Duccio di Buoninsegna

subchapters.title: The Wilton Diptych
subchapters.text: Look for the small hinged diptych made around 1395–99 for King Richard II's private prayers — two oak panels that close like a book. Inside, Richard kneels in cloth-of-gold, presented to the Virgin and Child by St Edmund, St Edward the Confessor and John the Baptist, while eleven angels crowd the Virgin's blue side wearing Richard's own badge, the white hart, and one holds the banner of St George. Outside, the white hart lies in a rosemary bed beneath Richard's arms. Nobody knows the artist's name — English or French — but the jewel-like surface, real gold and punched detail make it the supreme survival of the elegant International Gothic style, and a fragile piece of royal propaganda in paint.
subchapters.caption: The Wilton Diptych

subchapters.title: Saints You Can Recognise
subchapters.text: Medieval viewers read saints the way you read road signs — by their attributes. Look for Catherine with her spiked wheel, Margaret emerging from the dragon that swallowed her, Jerome in cardinal's red beating his breast with a stone, and Francis showing the stigmata, the wounds of Christ that appeared on his hands and feet. Sassetta's panels of St Francis, painted in the 1430s–40s for Sansepolcro, turn those signs into tender, quirky storytelling — Francis giving his cloak to a poor knight, or receiving the wounds in a rocky landscape. Learning two or three attributes transforms these rooms: suddenly every crowded altarpiece becomes a labelled gathering of individuals, each with a biography the first viewers knew by heart.
subchapters.caption: Saint Francis Receiving the Stigmata — Sassetta

subchapters.title: Panels, Predellas and Cassoni
subchapters.text: Notice the shapes. Tall central panels carried the main sacred figures; below them ran a predella, a strip of small narrative scenes like a comic strip for the illiterate; side panels could fold shut in Lent. Elsewhere, painted chests — cassoni — celebrated marriages, their fronts showing processions, battles and classical lovers in contemporary Florentine dress. Uccello's little St George and the Dragon, with its princess, storm-swirl and neat green maze of a landscape, may have decorated furniture rather than a church. These objects remind you that Renaissance painting lived on furniture, banners and birth trays as well as walls — the gallery has rescued the survivors and hung them at eye level.
subchapters.caption: Saint George and the Dragon — Paolo Uccello

subchapters.title: Pisanello and the Vision of Saint Eustace
subchapters.text: Find Pisanello's Vision of Saint Eustace, from around 1438–42, and enjoy a hunting scene turned vision. Eustace, a Roman general out hunting, kneels as a stag appears carrying a crucifix between its antlers — the moment of his conversion. Around him Pisanello packs an entire menagerie with jeweller's precision: hounds, a bear, cranes, swans and deer, each observed from life and set like enamel on the dark wood. Pisanello was also the age's great medallist, and it shows — every animal feels struck, crisp and collectable. It is a perfect bridge picture: medieval in its flat, tapestry richness, Renaissance in its loving observation of the natural world.
subchapters.caption: The Vision of Saint Eustace — Pisanello

chapters.title: Inventing Perspective — Florence Learns Depth
chapters.intro: Florence in the 1420s performed a magic trick: it made flat wood look deep. Brunelleschi's perspective experiments became, in painters' hands, a new way of organising both space and story. These rooms let you watch the trick being learned — lances, floors and riverbanks all pressed into service as measuring devices.

subchapters.title: Uccello — The Battle of San Romano
subchapters.text: Look for Paolo Uccello's Battle of San Romano, one of three huge panels — its companions are in the Louvre and the Uffizi — showing Florence's 1432 clash with Siena as a gorgeous, bloodless pageant. Broken lances lie on the ground in a near-perfect perspective grid, horses rear like rocking-horses, and the commander Niccolò da Tolentino, in a fabulous hat, directs traffic in the middle distance. Uccello was so obsessed with perspective that, his wife complained, he stayed up all night murmuring about vanishing points. Vasari thought the obsession damaged his art; standing here, enjoy it instead as pure intellectual pleasure — a battle reimagined as geometry, trumpets, heraldry and patterned oranges in the hedge beyond.
subchapters.directions: Stay in the Sainsbury Wing and work through the Florentine rooms.
subchapters.caption: The Battle of San Romano — Paolo Uccello

subchapters.title: Piero della Francesca — The Baptism of Christ
subchapters.text: In its chapel-like space, find Piero della Francesca's Baptism of Christ, painted in the late 1440s for his home town, Sansepolcro. Everything is stillness and measure: Christ stands in the Jordan — here a Tuscan stream that famously seems to stop flowing at his feet — while John pours water from a shell and three angels, dressed like Florentine youths, hold Christ's garment. A walnut tree divides the panel with mathematical calm, and a tiny reflected town glitters in the water. Piero wrote treatises on perspective and geometry, and this is mathematics become devotion: no drama, just light, order and quiet so complete you lower your voice in front of it.
subchapters.caption: The Baptism of Christ — Piero della Francesca

subchapters.title: Piero — The Nativity and the Unfinished Surface
subchapters.text: Nearby, Piero's Nativity, from about 1470–75, tells a stranger story. Angels sing from a rooftop — one plays a lute, mouths open in a choir you can almost hear — while Mary kneels on the ground in adoration and Joseph sits on a donkey's saddle, chatting. Look at the surface: parts are thin and worn, the paint damaged by early cleaning, which gives the picture its pale, fresco-like ghostliness. Piero, nearly blind at the end of his life, left a body of work so small and so lucid that modern painters from Seurat to Hockney have made pilgrimages to it. Compare the Nativity's bleached calm with the Baptism's enamel finish and you see both his range and the fragility of old paint.
subchapters.caption: The Nativity — Piero della Francesca

subchapters.title: Mantegna — The Agony in the Garden
subchapters.text: Andrea Mantegna brings a sculptor's hardness to the story. In his Agony in the Garden, around 1455–56, Christ prays on a rocky terrace while the disciples sleep in a heap below, their foreshortened bodies a deliberate show of skill, and tiny angels hold the instruments of the coming Passion. Across the valley a walled Jerusalem gleams, every tower counted. Mantegna, court painter at Mantua and brother-in-law to Giovanni Bellini, carved paint like marble — drapery falls in crisp, metallic folds. His Triumphs of Caesar cartoons, by the way, live at Hampton Court; here, this small panel and its companion pieces give you his essence: archaeology, discipline and drama held in perfect tension.
subchapters.caption: The Agony in the Garden — Andrea Mantegna

subchapters.title: Crivelli — The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius
subchapters.text: Carlo Crivelli's Annunciation of 1486 is the most exuberant picture in these rooms — and it hides a cucumber. The Virgin kneels in a marble loggia of impossible perspective luxury while the angel arrives outside; beside him St Emidius, patron of Ascoli Piceno, carries a model of the town, because the painting celebrates the town's self-government, announced on the feast of the Annunciation in 1482. Along the bottom, a cucumber and an apple cast real shadows over the frame's edge — the cucumber a symbol of resurrection, and a trompe-l'oeil joke about painting's power to fool you. Crivelli signed it, proudly, on a fake marble tablet. It is devotion, civic pride and showing off, all at once.
subchapters.caption: The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius — Carlo Crivelli

chapters.title: The Northern Eye — Van Eyck and the Arnolfini Portrait
chapters.intro: While Florence measured space, painters in Bruges were perfecting oil paint itself — slow-drying, translucent, able to render a brass chandelier, a fur trim and a distant window in one small panel. The North's gift to art is not perspective but attention, and its supreme exhibit is about the size of a television screen.

subchapters.title: Jan van Eyck — The Arnolfini Portrait
subchapters.text: Find the painting everyone comes to this wing for: Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait of 1434. The Bruges merchant Giovanni Arnolfini and his wife stand in a bedroom hung with a brass chandelier, oranges on the sill — luxury imports in Bruges — a little Brussels griffon at their feet and discarded clogs marking sacred ground. She gathers her green dress at her belly, a fashion gesture, not a pregnancy. Every surface is a demonstration of oil paint's new powers: fur, wood, metal, glass and cloth each rendered in their own light. Generations have read the picture as a painted marriage document; van Eyck certainly made it feel like sworn testimony, witnessed and signed.
subchapters.directions: Get close to the Arnolfini Portrait — the mirror is on the back wall, at the centre of the picture.
subchapters.caption: The Arnolfini Portrait — Jan van Eyck

subchapters.title: The Mirror and the Signature
subchapters.text: Now get close and find the convex mirror on the back wall, framed by ten tiny scenes of Christ's Passion. It reflects the entire room from behind — including two extra men entering the doorway, one in red who may be van Eyck himself. Above it, in elaborate Latin, the wall is signed not 'Jan van Eyck made this' but 'Johannes de Eyck fuit hic' — Jan van Eyck was here, 1434. A witness statement in paint, which is why scholars have long treated the panel as a visual record of a marriage or betrothal, the joined hands and raised palm reading as oaths. Whether document or portrait, no painting in Europe packs more looking into less space.
subchapters.caption: Detail: the convex mirror and signature, The Arnolfini Portrait — Jan van Eyck

subchapters.title: The Man in the Red Turban and Van Eyck's Portraits
subchapters.text: Look for the small Portrait of a Man in a Red Turban of 1433, quite possibly van Eyck's self-portrait — the steady, appraising stare feels like a painter studying himself in a mirror. Its frame carries his motto, 'Als ich can' — as best I can — a pun on his name in Flemish. Van Eyck served Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, as court painter and occasional diplomatic envoy, and his portraits set the Northern standard: no flattery, every wrinkle and stubble hair admitted, personality built from scrutiny. Compare this head with any Italian profile portrait nearby and you feel two Renaissances regarding each other across the Alps — one idealising, one inspecting.
subchapters.caption: Portrait of a Man (Self Portrait?) — Jan van Eyck

subchapters.title: Rogier van der Weyden and Memling
subchapters.text: Rogier van der Weyden, van Eyck's great contemporary, traded optical fireworks for emotion. His Magdalene Reading, a fragment of a larger altarpiece, shows a young woman in white absorbed in a book, her lowered eyes and the exquisite still life of her jar and beads creating a hush you can feel across the room. A generation later, Hans Memling perfected Bruges painting for export — serene Madonnas, donors kneeling in polished interiors, landscapes glimpsed through loggias. The Donne Triptych, painted for the Welsh courtier Sir John Donne on a visit to Bruges, shows how far this art travelled: a Welsh knight, his wife and daughter, presented to the Virgin in a Flemish interior, saints and angels in attendance.
subchapters.caption: The Magdalen Reading — Rogier van der Weyden

subchapters.title: Massys — The Ugly Duchess
subchapters.text: For Northern wit at full strength, find Quinten Massys's portrait known as The Ugly Duchess, around 1513. An elderly woman in the headdress and low-cut dress of her youth offers a rosebud, the traditional token of love, to an unseen suitor. It is usually read as satire — a warning against vanity and age dressing young — possibly after Erasmus's Praise of Folly, and the picture became so famous that John Tenniel borrowed the face for the Duchess in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. But look at the painting itself, not just the joke: the wrinkled skin, snub nose and lively eyes are painted with the same merciless tenderness van Eyck taught the North. Satire, here, is a form of attention.
subchapters.caption: An Old Woman (The Ugly Duchess) — Quinten Massys

chapters.caption: Jan van Eyck, The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) — the mirror that sees everything

chapters.title: Botticelli — Line, Myth and Venus and Mars
chapters.intro: Sandro Botticelli painted for the Medici's Florence a world of dancing line and learned myth — pictures meant for bedrooms and wedding chambers, full of philosophy disguised as pretty gods. His contour flows like handwriting; even a sleeping war god looks ready to drift off the panel in a ribbon of drapery.

subchapters.title: Venus and Mars
subchapters.text: Find Venus and Mars, painted around 1485, and enjoy one of the slyest pictures of the Renaissance. Mars, god of war, is fast asleep, utterly knocked out after lovemaking, while little satyrs play with his armour — one blows a conch shell in his ear and he doesn't stir, another hauls away his lance, a third has crawled inside his breastplate. Venus sits wide awake, serene and completely in charge. For the Florentine household this was probably painted for — likely as a wedding picture, perhaps for a bed or bench panel — the message is clear and cheering: love conquers war. Botticelli paints the whole joke in that flowing, calligraphic line that makes everything look like it's dancing, even a snoring god.
subchapters.caption: Venus and Mars — Sandro Botticelli

subchapters.title: The Wasps in the Corner
subchapters.text: Before you move on, look for the detail most visitors miss, down by Mars's head: wasps are nesting in the hollow of a tree trunk in the bottom right corner. Wasps — vespe in Italian — were the emblem of the Vespucci family, the Florentine clan that gave its name to America through Amerigo Vespucci, and a delicious visual pun for the probable patrons. There may be a second meaning too: love, however sweet, has a sting, and the wasps hover beside the sleeper's ear as a small warning inside the compliment. This is how Renaissance pictures worked — a public story on the surface, and private heraldry, jokes and morals tucked into the corners for those who knew the family.
subchapters.caption: Detail: Mars asleep, with wasps nesting beside his head, Venus and Mars — Sandro Botticelli

subchapters.title: The Mystic Nativity
subchapters.text: Botticelli's Mystic Nativity, signed and dated 1500, is the opposite of a charmer — deliberately. Painted in the anxious aftermath of the preacher Savonarola's fall, it carries a long Greek inscription across the top in which Botticelli links the scene to the Book of Revelation and the troubles of Italy. Angels dance on the stable roof, demons flee into cracks in the earth, and three pairs of men and angels embrace in the foreground as if reconciling heaven and earth. It is the only picture Botticelli signed, and its deliberate archaism — gold ground creeping back in at the edges — shows an artist retreating from Renaissance confidence into prophecy as the century turned.
subchapters.caption: The Mystic Nativity — Sandro Botticelli

subchapters.title: Botticelli's Madonnas and the Medici Circle
subchapters.text: Around the mythologies hang Botticelli's Madonnas, and they teach you his other register: tenderness engineered by line. In the Madonna of the Pomegranate type and its cousins, the Virgin's long fingers, the child's solemnity and the circling angels all turn on that same unbroken contour. These pictures were produced by a busy workshop for Florentine homes — devotion for the bedchamber — yet the best are autograph poetry. Remember Botticelli worked steps from power: the Medici, the Tornabuoni, the Vespucci. His Primavera and Birth of Venus hang in the Uffizi, but London's share — intimate, witty, domestic — shows the side of him Florentines actually lived with, over their beds and benches.
subchapters.caption: The Virgin and Child with a Pomegranate — workshop of Sandro Botticelli

subchapters.title: Mars, Venus and the Wedding Chamber
subchapters.text: Step back and place Venus and Mars where it first lived. Long, low mythologies like this were painted for spalliere — panels set into bedroom furniture or wainscoting — or for the backs and fronts of wedding chests, so the first viewers saw them reclining, at pillow height, in a room made for a marriage. That explains the picture's horizontal languor, its joke about a warrior disarmed in a bedroom, and its moralising tenderness. When you meet other long panels in these rooms — processions, hunts, the story of Nastagio degli Onesti's grisly forest banquet — read them the same way: furniture that talked, telling newlyweds how to live, love and behave, in pictures.

chapters.caption: Botticelli's Venus and Mars (c. 1485) — love conquers war, with wasps

chapters.title: Leonardo — The Virgin of the Rocks
chapters.intro: In a dimmer room hangs painting slowed down to the speed of thought. Leonardo worked on this picture, on and off, for over twenty years, and it shows — every face emerges from shadow the way an idea emerges in the mind. Give this chapter unhurried time; it repays silence.

subchapters.title: The Virgin of the Rocks
subchapters.text: The scene is an invented legend — the young John the Baptist meeting the Christ Child in the wilderness — set not in a landscape but in a shadowy grotto of wet rocks and strange, botanically exact flowers, lit by something between daylight and a dream. Mary reaches protectively over the infant John, who prays toward Jesus; Jesus, a toddler, raises two fingers in blessing; and an angel kneels behind, pointing, and looking straight out at you with an expression argued about for 500 years. There are two versions of the composition — this London one, begun around 1491, and an earlier one in the Louvre — and the current scholarly view credits Leonardo with more of this version's painting than was once thought.
subchapters.directions: From Botticelli, continue to the Leonardo room in the Sainsbury Wing.
subchapters.caption: The Virgin of the Rocks — Leonardo da Vinci

subchapters.title: Sfumato — Painting in Smoke
subchapters.text: Everything here is Leonardo's signature technique: sfumato, from sfumare, to vanish like smoke. Corners of eyes and mouths have no hard edge at all; form is modelled in transitions so soft that the faces seem to breathe. Leonardo wrote that shadows should have no lines, because in nature they don't, and he built up paint in glazes thinner than a breath to prove it. Try the experiment yourself: cover the angel's face except for the mouth, then except for the eyes, and watch the expression change. That deliberate ambiguity — a smile that is also a warning — is the invention that made Leonardo's portraits, above all the Mona Lisa, into permanent mysteries.
subchapters.caption: Detail: the angel, The Virgin of the Rocks — Leonardo da Vinci

subchapters.title: The Burlington House Cartoon
subchapters.text: Don't miss the Burlington House Cartoon nearby: a huge drawing in charcoal and white chalk, about a metre and a half wide, of the Virgin and Child with St Anne and the infant John, made around 1499–1500. It is the only large Leonardo drawing to survive, and you are looking at his actual hand moving across joined sheets of paper five centuries ago — searching, adjusting, letting a knee or a pointing finger emerge from the haze. A cartoon was a working tool, meant to be pricked and transferred to a panel; that this one was never used, and was treasured instead, tells you contemporaries already treated Leonardo's drawings as relics. For many visitors it is the most quietly thrilling object in the building.
subchapters.caption: The Burlington House Cartoon (The Virgin and Child with Saint Anne and Saint John the Baptist) — Leonardo da Vinci

subchapters.title: Leonardo the Scientist in the Grotto
subchapters.text: Look at the grotto itself with a geologist's eye, because Leonardo did. The stratified rocks, the pool, the distant blue crags and the plants — iris, columbine, violets — are observed with the same curiosity he poured into his notebooks on water, fossils and anatomy. He had found fossil shells in mountains and concluded, correctly, that seas had once covered them, against the teaching of his day. In this picture the Virgin sits inside that deep time, among rocks older than any doctrine. Leonardo never separated art from investigation: the same man dissected corpses, designed flying machines and painted this angel. The grotto is his laboratory disguised as a shrine.
subchapters.caption: Detail: the grotto rocks, The Virgin of the Rocks — Leonardo da Vinci

subchapters.title: Why Two Versions Exist
subchapters.text: The puzzle of the two Virgin of the Rocks panels is a lesson in Renaissance business. The London picture was painted for a Milanese confraternity's altarpiece in the church of San Francesco Grande, under a contract of 1483 — but a long payment dispute followed, and the first version was likely sold elsewhere, ending in the Louvre. Leonardo and his partners then supplied this second painting, delivered by about 1508, with workshop help in places and the master's hand unmistakable in the heads and the angel. X-rays and infrared studies show changes and underdrawing that have kept scholars busy for decades. Stand here knowing you are looking not at a copy, but at a negotiation — in paint.
subchapters.caption: The Virgin of the Rocks (the Louvre version) — Leonardo da Vinci

chapters.caption: Leonardo da Vinci, The Virgin of the Rocks (c. 1491–1508)

chapters.title: Michelangelo and Raphael — The High Renaissance
chapters.intro: Cross into the 1500s and the temperature rises. Rome around 1500 concentrated genius the way a lens concentrates light, and these rooms stage its defining contrast: Michelangelo, the sculptor who painted reluctantly and left things unfinished, against Raphael, who finished everything and made perfection look easy.

subchapters.title: Michelangelo — The Entombment
subchapters.text: Michelangelo's Entombment, from about 1500–01, is one of only a handful of his panel paintings — and it is unfinished, which is precisely why you should linger. Christ's body is carried by solemn figures against a landscape that stops mid-thought: areas of bare preparation, drapery resolved in one place and sketched in another, a gap where further figures were planned. You are watching the greatest sculptor of the age think in paint in his mid-twenties, then abandon the panel — probably because Rome, Pope Julius II and marble were calling. Within a few years he would carve the David and begin the Sistine ceiling. The unfinished state is a gift: process, usually hidden, is the exhibit.
subchapters.directions: Continue into the High Renaissance rooms.
subchapters.caption: The Entombment — Michelangelo

subchapters.title: Michelangelo — The Manchester Madonna
subchapters.text: Nearby hangs the earlier Madonna and Child with Saint John, known as the Manchester Madonna, from about 1497, when Michelangelo was barely twenty-two. It is also unfinished — the angels at the sides are blocked in with a greenish underpaint and never completed — and it shows the young artist digesting his Florentine teachers, Domenico Ghirlandaio's workshop among them. Mary's twisting pose already has sculptural torque, and the Christ Child steps forward with a confidence no toddler should have. Bought in Manchester in the 19th century as a curiosity and only later recognised, the picture's very incompleteness helped scholars authenticate it: fakes are finished; experiments get abandoned when a better commission arrives.
subchapters.caption: The Manchester Madonna (Madonna and Child with Saint John and Angels) — Michelangelo

subchapters.title: Raphael — The Ansidei and Garvagh Madonnas
subchapters.text: Raphael, a few years younger than Michelangelo, is the opposite experience: everything finished, balanced, serene. The Ansidei Madonna of 1505 still keeps its altarpiece shape and its patron saint, Nicholas of Bari, reading beside the throne; the Garvagh Madonna, a few years later, loosens into pure tenderness — Mary in pink and blue, the two children bound in one flowing group. Raphael absorbed Leonardo's softness and Michelangelo's grandeur without copying either, which is why contemporaries thought he had achieved perfection itself. He ran the busiest workshop in Rome, painted the Pope's apartments, and died in 1520 at just thirty-seven, mourned like a prince. These calm Madonnas are the foundation that fame was built on.
subchapters.caption: The Ansidei Madonna — Raphael

subchapters.title: Raphael — The Madonna of the Pinks and Pope Julius II
subchapters.text: Two smaller Raphaels reward close looking. The Madonna of the Pinks, about 1506–07, shows Mary offering the child a carnation — a 'pink', symbol of divine love — in an interior so intimate it feels like a portrait sitting; the picture was long known only from copies until the original was recognised at Alnwick Castle and bought for the nation in 2004. Then find Raphael's Portrait of Pope Julius II of 1511–12: the warrior-pope who commissioned the Sistine ceiling, slumped in thought in his chair, acorns of his della Rovere family embroidered on the fabric behind him. It virtually invented the state portrait — every seated ruler since owes it something.
subchapters.caption: The Madonna of the Pinks — Raphael

subchapters.title: Cranach, Dürer and the German North
subchapters.text: The High Renaissance had a German accent too. Lucas Cranach the Elder, court painter at Wittenberg and friend of Martin Luther, fills his panels with spidery elegance — look for his Adam and Eve or the Portrait of Erasmus, all enamel surface and sly intelligence. Albrecht Dürer, the North's Leonardo, is represented by works including St Jerome in the Wilderness, the saint beating his breast in a landscape studied from nature. Dürer travelled to Italy twice precisely to learn what Raphael knew, then carried perspective and anatomy home in prints that spread the Renaissance across Europe. These rooms are where the two Renaissances — Italian and Northern — finally shake hands.
subchapters.caption: Saint Jerome in the Wilderness — Albrecht Dürer

chapters.title: Holbein and the Tudor Court
chapters.intro: Hans Holbein the Younger arrived in London with a letter from Erasmus and left behind the defining images of Henry VIII's court — portraits so exact you can read the embroidery, and one picture with a magic trick hidden across its foreground. Northern precision, here, serves Tudor power.

subchapters.title: The Ambassadors
subchapters.text: Find The Ambassadors of 1533, Holbein's double portrait of Jean de Dinteville, French ambassador to Henry VIII's court, and Georges de Selve, bishop and fellow diplomat. Between them stands a two-shelf still life of power and learning: celestial and terrestrial globes, sundials, a torquetum, books, a lute with a broken string — often read as religious discord in the year of Henry's break with Rome — and a Lutheran hymnal. The carpet, the silver, the dagger ages inscribed on their sheaths: everything declares rank and accomplishment. It is a portrait of two men, and also an inventory of everything a Renaissance courtier was supposed to know.
subchapters.directions: Look at The Ambassadors from low down at the far right side — stand there and watch the foreground smear resolve.
subchapters.caption: The Ambassadors — Hans Holbein the Younger

subchapters.title: The Skull in Plain Sight
subchapters.text: Now perform the gallery's best magic trick. Across the foreground floats a grey smear, deliberately unreadable from the front. Walk to the right side of the picture, crouch slightly, and look back along the surface at a sharp angle: the smear snaps into a perfect human skull, grinning across the parquet. This is anamorphosis — perspective weaponised — and the skull is a memento mori, a reminder of death placed inside a picture otherwise devoted to worldly achievement. A small crucifix half-hides behind the curtain at top left, the picture's quiet answer to its own skull. Tudor viewers, who loved devices and conceits, would have delighted in being made to move to get the point.
subchapters.caption: Detail: the anamorphic skull, The Ambassadors — Hans Holbein the Younger

subchapters.title: Christina of Denmark and the Tudor Portraits
subchapters.text: Holbein's Christina of Denmark, painted in 1538, was made as diplomatic evidence: Henry VIII, widowed, was shopping for a fourth wife, and Holbein was sent to Brussels to paint the sixteen-year-old duchess — in mourning black, with a shy, appraising intelligence that fills the full-length canvas. The marriage never happened; Christina reportedly said she would offer two heads if she had them, knowing Anne Boleyn's fate. Around these set pieces hang Holbein's smaller portraits — Erasmus, Thomas More's circle, merchants of the Steelyard — each face built from a chalk drawing so precise that the painted version needed only to keep faith with it. This is portraiture as intelligence-gathering.
subchapters.caption: Christina of Denmark, Duchess of Milan — Hans Holbein the Younger

subchapters.title: The Execution of Lady Jane Grey — A Later History
subchapters.text: In the later British and French rooms you will meet Paul Delaroche's Execution of Lady Jane Grey of 1833, a Frenchman's theatrical vision of Tudor tragedy: the seventeen-year-old queen, blindfolded, feeling for the block in a darkened Tower chamber while her ladies collapse around her. Jane reigned nine days in 1553 before Mary Tudor took the throne. Delaroche's picture is history painting as cinema — historically loose, emotionally exact — and it became one of the most famous images of the 19th century. Pair it mentally with Holbein: the Tudor court painted from life in one room, and reimagined in costume drama, three centuries later, in another.
subchapters.caption: The Execution of Lady Jane Grey — Paul Delaroche

chapters.caption: Holbein, The Ambassadors (1533) — Tudor power, learning and a hidden skull

chapters.title: Venice — Titian, Veronese and the Colour of Power
chapters.intro: Venice painted differently: in oil on canvas, in a damp sea light, with pigments traded through its own port — ultramarine from Afghanistan, reds from the East. Venetians said disegno, drawing, was Florence's game; theirs was colorito, colour itself, and these rooms are their winning argument.

subchapters.title: Titian — Bacchus and Ariadne
subchapters.text: If Leonardo is smoke, Titian is fireworks. Bacchus and Ariadne, painted in 1520–23 for the Duke of Ferrara's private study, may be the most joyful painting in the building. Ariadne, abandoned on Naxos by Theseus — that is his ship sailing away on the left — is startled by Bacchus, god of wine, leaping from his cheetah-drawn chariot, so in love at first sight he is frozen mid-air, drapery flying. Above her head glitter the stars her crown will become. But the story is an excuse for the colour: that sky is ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli, more expensive than gold, laid on like Titian owned the mine, and the whole canvas choreographs reds, whites and blues around it.
subchapters.caption: Bacchus and Ariadne — Titian

subchapters.title: Titian — Death of Actaeon and Diana
subchapters.text: Titian painted into his eighties, and his late style dissolves form into pure, rough paint. The Death of Actaeon, never quite finished and never delivered in his lifetime, shows the hunter who surprised Diana bathing being torn apart by his own hounds — Diana drawing her bow at the left, Actaeon already half-stag, the whole scene a shimmer of brown and gold brushwork that anticipates Impressionism by three centuries. It was saved for the nation in 1972 after a famous public appeal. Nearby, Diana and Callisto tells the companion myth with the same late looseness. Stand close and the pictures nearly vanish into strokes; step back and they ignite. That double experience is modern painting being born.
subchapters.caption: The Death of Actaeon — Titian

subchapters.title: Veronese — The Family of Darius and the Allegories
subchapters.text: Paolo Veronese painted Venice's fantasy of itself: marble terraces, silk, silver and crowds arranged like opera sets. The Family of Darius before Alexander, a vast canvas of the 1560s, shows Alexander the Great graciously receiving the captured family of the Persian king he defeated — but the Persians wear Venetian brocade, the architecture is Palladian, and a little dog and a dwarf hold the foreground. Veronese's Four Allegories of Love, painted as ceiling pieces, float gods and lovers in pearly light. His gift was splendour without heaviness; even a surrender looks like a festival. When the Inquisition objected to the company in one of his Last Suppers, he simply retitled it Feast in the House of Levi — Venetian pragmatism in one gesture.
subchapters.caption: The Family of Darius before Alexander — Paolo Veronese

subchapters.title: Tintoretto and the Venetian Drama
subchapters.text: Jacopo Tintoretto, dyer's son, worked fast, dark and theatrical — his nickname was il Furioso for the fury of his painting. His Origin of the Milky Way, about 1575, retells how Jupiter placed the infant Hercules at the sleeping Juno's breast, her spilt milk spraying into stars above and lilies below; the picture was cut down in the past and still feels explosive. Tintoretto's steep perspectives and plunging diagonals were designed to overwhelm, and in the huge canvases of St George and the Dragon the saint arrives like a cavalry charge. Set his turbulence beside Titian's glow and Veronese's pageantry and you have Venice's three temperaments, arguing in paint across one set of rooms.
subchapters.caption: The Origin of the Milky Way — Tintoretto

subchapters.title: Giorgione and the Pastoral Mystery
subchapters.text: Smallest and rarest here is Giorgione, who died around 1510 in his early thirties leaving a handful of poetic, puzzling pictures that changed art. The gallery's works associated with him and his circle — shepherds in golden landscapes, the Adoration of the Kings, the sunset glow known as Il Tramonto — replace story with mood: figures pause, music is implied, nobody explains anything. Titian finished some of these canvases after Giorgione's death, and scholars still argue over where one hand stops and the other starts. That uncertainty is fitting. Giorgione invented the easel picture as a daydream, and Venice — and then Europe — spent centuries dreaming in his format.
subchapters.caption: Il Tramonto (The Sunset) — Giorgione

chapters.caption: Titian, Bacchus and Ariadne (1520–23) — Venetian colour at full blast

chapters.title: Baroque Drama — Caravaggio, Rubens and Velázquez
chapters.intro: Around 1600 painting learned theatre. Caravaggio lit sacred stories like street brawls, Rubens set flesh and silk in motion, and Velázquez, quietest of all, made a mirror do the philosophising. These rooms hold one supreme example of each — plus the only female nude by Spain's greatest painter.

subchapters.title: Caravaggio — The Supper at Emmaus
subchapters.text: Caravaggio's Supper at Emmaus of 1601 catches the instant the resurrected Christ, beardless and ordinary, blesses bread and is recognised by his two disciples — one throws his arms wide, the other grips his chair, half-rising, while the innkeeper, oblivious, looks on. Caravaggio paints revelation as a tavern moment, lit hard from the left, with a basket of fruit teetering over the table's edge straight toward you. He used live models off the street and no preparatory drawings, which scandalised Rome and electrified it. The gallery also holds his boyish Boy Bitten by a Lizard and the late, exhausted Salome with the Head of John the Baptist — a short career, 1571 to 1610, that permanently changed painting's lighting.
subchapters.directions: Look for the Baroque rooms in the North Wing.
subchapters.caption: The Supper at Emmaus — Caravaggio

subchapters.title: Rubens — Samson and Delilah
subchapters.text: Peter Paul Rubens painted Samson and Delilah about 1609–10, fresh from Italy and drunk on Caravaggio and Michelangelo. Samson sleeps across Delilah's lap in a candlelit interior while a servant clips his hair — crossing his hands as he cuts, an old sign of betrayal — an old woman lends extra light, and Philistine soldiers wait in the doorway under a statue of Venus, the cause of it all. The picture was commissioned by Nicolaas Rockox, burgomaster of Antwerp, for his own house. Everything is sumptuous and doomed: satin, skin, armour and that cascade of red drapery. Its attribution has been debated by campaigners for decades; the gallery stands by Rubens, and the paint handling — confident, sculptural, sensuous — argues with them.
subchapters.caption: Samson and Delilah — Peter Paul Rubens

subchapters.title: Rubens — Het Steen, the Judgement of Paris and Le Chapeau de Paille
subchapters.text: Rubens the diplomat-painter also painted peace. A View of Het Steen, about 1636, shows the country estate he bought near Brussels, in golden morning light, a hunter setting out, cattle grazing — a successful man's contentment spread across a panorama, its companion Rainbow Landscape hanging in the Wallace Collection. His Judgement of Paris stages the beauty contest that started the Trojan War as a swirl of goddesses, and Le Chapeau de Paille — the straw hat — is really a portrait of Susanna Lunden in a feathered hat, so luminous that painters copied it for two centuries. Rubens ran Europe's most efficient studio and still found time to be its busiest ambassador; these pictures show both the factory and the man.
subchapters.caption: A View of Het Steen in the Early Morning — Peter Paul Rubens

subchapters.title: Velázquez — The Rokeby Venus
subchapters.text: Diego Velázquez's Rokeby Venus, painted 1647–51, is his only surviving female nude — a subject the Spanish Inquisition made nearly impossible at home, painted probably for a private patron and kept behind curtains. Venus lies with her back to us, Cupid holding a mirror in which her blurred face looks out, so she watches you watching her. The paint is miraculously spare: a grey sheet, a dark curtain, flesh modelled in a few warm tones. The picture's modern fame includes violence — on 10 March 1914 the suffragette Mary Richardson slashed it with a meat chopper in protest at Emmeline Pankhurst's arrest; the wounds were repaired, and close looking still finds their traces in the surface.
subchapters.caption: The Rokeby Venus (Venus at her Mirror) — Diego Velázquez

subchapters.title: Velázquez Portraits and Artemisia Gentileschi
subchapters.text: Velázquez also painted power undressed of ceremony: his Philip IV in Brown and Silver shows the king of Spain in hunting dress, a study in weary understatement, and Christ in the House of Martha and Mary smuggles a kitchen scene into a religious picture. Near them, seek Artemisia Gentileschi's Self-Portrait as Saint Catherine of Alexandria, about 1615–17 — the artist leaning on Catherine's broken wheel, palm of martyrdom in hand, meeting your eye with level self-possession. Gentileschi, trained by her father Orazio and famous in her lifetime across Naples, Rome and London, was rediscovered by the 20th century; the gallery bought this picture in 2018, its first work by a woman artist in decades, and it now holds its own in the toughest room in the building.
subchapters.caption: Self-Portrait as Saint Catherine of Alexandria — Artemisia Gentileschi

chapters.title: Dutch Quiet — Vermeer, Rembrandt and the Golden Age
chapters.intro: The 17th-century Dutch Republic, rich on trade and short on palaces, painted small: interiors, landscapes, still lifes for merchants' walls. At one extreme, Vermeer's silence; at the other, Rembrandt's theatre of the soul. Between them, a whole society inventories itself — skaters, lutes, lobsters, and light.

subchapters.title: Vermeer — A Lady Standing at a Virginal
subchapters.text: Johannes Vermeer's A Lady Standing at a Virginal, about 1670–72, shows a young woman pausing at a keyboard instrument in a tiled Delft interior, a painting of Cupid on the wall behind her and daylight — always from the left — washing across the scene. Its companion, A Lady Seated at a Virginal, hangs with it; the two were probably painted as a pair. There are only about 37 Vermeers in the world. Notice how he builds psychology from geometry: the virginal's decorated lid, the chair, the picture-within-the-picture, a woman mid-thought with music suspended. Nothing happens, and somehow everything happens. Vermeer died at forty-two leaving debts; these two calm rooms are now beyond price.
subchapters.directions: Continue to the Dutch rooms in the North Wing.
subchapters.caption: A Lady Standing at a Virginal — Johannes Vermeer

subchapters.title: Rembrandt — Self-Portrait at the Age of 34
subchapters.text: Find Rembrandt's Self Portrait at the Age of 34, painted in 1640 at the height of his fame and fortune. He presents himself in rich dress, arm resting on a parapet in a pose borrowed deliberately from Raphael's Baldassarre Castiglione and Titian's Man with a Quilted Sleeve — a young master composing his own legend by quoting the old ones. He was Amsterdam's most fashionable portraitist, owner of a grand house and a famous collection, married to Saskia. The paint is still relatively smooth, the confidence total. Keep this face in your mind; you are about to meet it again twenty-nine years later, in the same collection, and the distance between the two pictures is one of the great experiences this gallery offers.
subchapters.caption: Self-Portrait at the Age of 34 — Rembrandt

subchapters.title: Rembrandt — Self-Portrait at the Age of 63
subchapters.text: Now find the Self Portrait at the Age of 63, from 1669, the year of his death. Saskia is long dead, then Hendrickje; the house and collection were sold for bankruptcy in the 1650s; commissions had thinned. And the painting is freer and greater than the young man's — paint built up like sculpture, the face emerging from darkness with clasped hands and a white cap, honesty replacing theatre. Rembrandt painted, drew and etched himself around eighty times, an autobiography without words. Stand between the two self-portraits for a while. Same man, same museum, twenty-nine years apart: ambition at one end, wisdom at the other, and no self-pity anywhere. It is the most human moment in the gallery.
subchapters.caption: Self-Portrait at the Age of 63 — Rembrandt

subchapters.title: Rembrandt — Belshazzar's Feast and Bathsheba
subchapters.text: Rembrandt could also do spectacle. Belshazzar's Feast, about 1636–38, freezes the Babylonian king recoiling as a disembodied hand writes the warning on his palace wall — MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN — the letters in Hebrew characters, arranged, scholars note, in columns as a rabbi friend may have advised. Gold vessels looted from the Temple, a terrified court, and light like a struck match. Quieter and deeper is Bathsheba at her Bath of 1654 in the Louvre — here, look instead for the gallery's other Rembrandt histories and portraits, including his portrait of Saskia's cousin Aechje Claesdr and the tender Margaretha de Geer. His range in one room: apocalypse and intimacy from the same brush.
subchapters.caption: Belshazzar's Feast — Rembrandt

subchapters.title: Dutch Landscapes, Still Life and the Avenue at Middelharnis
subchapters.text: Finish the Dutch rooms outdoors, so to speak. Meindert Hobbema's Avenue at Middelharnis of 1689 is one of the most famous landscapes in art — a dead-straight road of young pollarded trees receding to a village, a man pruning, a couple strolling, painted when Hobbema had largely given up art for a tax job. Aelbert Cuyp bathes Dordrecht in Italian gold he never saw in Italy, Jacob van Ruisdael broods over Haarlem under enormous skies, and the still-life tables groan with pewter, lemons and cut tulips — wealth rendered perishable on purpose. These were pictures for houses like the ones they depict: a merchant republic admiring, and gently moralising, itself.
subchapters.caption: The Avenue at Middelharnis — Meindert Hobbema

chapters.caption: Rembrandt's self-portraits — a whole life, painted honestly

chapters.title: Venice Again and French Calm — Canaletto, Poussin and Claude
chapters.intro: Cross the Central Hall and the light changes again. Venetian view-painters are selling Venice to tourists, while in Rome two Frenchmen, Poussin and Claude, are inventing the classical landscape — one all reason and moral story, the other all golden air. Both exports shaped Britain's taste for a century.

subchapters.title: Canaletto — The Stonemason's Yard
subchapters.text: Canaletto's Stonemason's Yard, about 1725, is his masterpiece precisely because it is not a postcard. Instead of the Grand Canal's palaces, you get a working yard at dawn on a side canal: masons chipping stone, a woman spinning, a child, washing hung out, the church of the Carità unfinished across the water. Canaletto — Giovanni Antonio Canal — built his views with a draughtsman's rigour, probably using a camera obscura for the architecture, then populated them with observed Venetian life. British tourists on the Grand Tour bought his festival views by the dozen; this quiet one, kept in Venice, shows what he could do when nobody asked for a souvenir.
subchapters.directions: Look for the Venetian view rooms and the French classical landscapes.
subchapters.caption: The Stonemason's Yard — Canaletto

subchapters.title: Canaletto in London and Guardi
subchapters.text: When war cut off the tourist trade in the 1740s, Canaletto simply moved to his market: he spent 1746 to 1756 in London painting the Thames — Westminster Bridge new and gleaming, processions of the Lord Mayor, the river as busy as the Grand Canal. Back in Venice, Francesco Guardi loosened the view into shimmer, his lagoons and capricci — invented ruins in golden light — pointing toward Impressionism. Together in these rooms, uncle-in-law and heir map a whole industry: Venice selling its own image to Europe. The pictures were so successful that 'Canaletto' became a generic word for a view; the Stonemason's Yard is your proof the man behind the brand was a great painter, not a brand at all.
subchapters.caption: Eton College Chapel — Canaletto

subchapters.title: Poussin — Order and Moral Story
subchapters.text: Nicolas Poussin, a Frenchman who spent his life in Rome, painted as if composing philosophy. In The Adoration of the Golden Calf and his Bacchanals and sacrament scenes, every gesture is placed like a word in a sentence: Israelites dance around their idol in a frieze of beautiful, damning movement while Moses descends with the tablets. Poussin read the story, chose the exact instant, and choreographed it — his method, mocked by rivals as painting for readers, set the standard for European history painting for two centuries. The gallery's Poussins reward slow, literate looking: identify each figure's role, and the picture's moral machinery starts to turn, gear by gear, exactly as designed.
subchapters.caption: The Adoration of the Golden Calf — Nicolas Poussin

subchapters.title: Claude — Golden Light and the Ideal Landscape
subchapters.text: Claude Lorrain, Poussin's Rome contemporary, painted the same classical world at the opposite temperature. His seaports and pastorals — The Enchanted Castle, landscapes with Psyche, Jacob, or Aeneas — dissolve architecture, water and tiny staffage figures into one honeyed, late-afternoon glow, usually with the sun placed just where it will melt the horizon. English aristocrats fell hardest for Claude: they bought him by the roomful, then went home and remodelled their estates to look like his pictures, lakes, temples, clumps and all. Turner, coming later in our route, worshipped him — and arranged, in his will, to hang beside him forever. You will see whether the pupil kept up.
subchapters.caption: The Enchanted Castle — Claude Lorrain

subchapters.title: French Portraiture and Chardin's Quiet
subchapters.text: French painting here is not only classical. Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin painted the anti-spectacle: The Young Schoolmistress, a girl patiently teaching a child its letters, and still lifes of kitchen copper and fruit, built from paint so sensitively handled that Diderot called him a magician. Nearby, the grand manner returns in portraits by Rigaud and Largillière, all silk and command, and in Watteau's early fête galante reveries, aristocrats flirting in parks at dusk. Hold Chardin's hush in mind as a palate cleanser between centuries: after courts and myths, a small girl, a slate, and complete attention — France's other gift to painting, intimacy.
subchapters.caption: The Young Schoolmistress — Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin

chapters.title: British Beginnings — Hogarth, Gainsborough and Stubbs
chapters.intro: Britain arrived late to great painting and then, characteristically, did it differently: satire you read like a novel, portraits rooted in real fields, and a horse painted like a god. These rooms hold the founding generation of the British School — several of them here since the gallery's first purchase in 1824.

subchapters.title: Hogarth — Marriage A-la-Mode
subchapters.text: William Hogarth's Marriage A-la-Mode, about 1743, is six paintings telling one disastrous story: a gouty earl marries his son to a merchant's daughter for money; the couple stray; there is a quack doctor, a murder in a bagnio, a suicide, and a final scene of the bride dying as her father pulls the ring from her finger. Every object testifies — the paintings on the walls, the spots of disease, the neglected child playing with a top. Hogarth called them his 'modern moral subjects', sold the engravings by subscription like a bestselling novel, and effectively invented British narrative art. The series was among the 38 pictures bought in 1824: the National Gallery began, in part, with a satire.
subchapters.directions: Find the British rooms in the East Wing.
subchapters.caption: Marriage A-la-Mode: The Tête à Tête — William Hogarth

subchapters.title: Hogarth — The Shrimp Girl and the Graham Children
subchapters.text: Hogarth was not only a moralist. The Shrimp Girl, about 1740–45, is a rapid oil sketch of a young street seller balancing her basket, painted with a freedom that anticipates the Impressionists — Hogarth's widow treasured it as proof of his hand. The Graham Children of 1742 shows apothecary Daniel Graham's children in silk and silver with a cat eyeing their caged bird — a group portrait shadowed by the fact that the baby, Thomas, had already died when it was painted; the cherub on the clock holds a scythe. Hogarth's world is London entire: commerce, childhood, disease, wit, all painted from observation rather than the antique. He also, tirelessly, campaigned for British artists — this gallery is partly his monument.
subchapters.caption: The Shrimp Girl — William Hogarth

subchapters.title: Gainsborough — Mr and Mrs Andrews
subchapters.text: Thomas Gainsborough painted Mr and Mrs Andrews about 1750, early in his career, in his native Suffolk: Robert Andrews and Frances Carter, newly married, pose in front of their own land — wheat sheaves, fenced fields, an oak, the church towers of Sudbury beyond — in a picture that is half portrait, half landscape, wholly about property and pride. Her lap holds an unfinished patch of paint, perhaps meant for a child or a pheasant. Gainsborough always said landscape was his love and portraiture his living; here the two are perfectly married, like the sitters. Compare the loose, feathery trees with Constable, coming soon: Suffolk painting has a family line, and it starts in this canvas.
subchapters.caption: Mr and Mrs Andrews — Thomas Gainsborough

subchapters.title: Gainsborough — The Morning Walk and the Painter's Daughters
subchapters.text: Later Gainsborough is all movement and shimmer. The Morning Walk of 1785 shows Mr and Mrs Hallett strolling with a white Pomeranian through feathery woodland, the paint dissolving into air — Gainsborough in London, rival to Reynolds, painting fashionable society as if it were weather. Sweetest of all are The Painter's Daughters chasing a Butterfly, about 1756: Mary and Margaret in a dark wood, hands joined, reaching for a cabbage white — a picture about childhood's briefness by a father who lost other children young. Gainsborough worked fast, with long brushes, muttering that painting was his mistress. The feathery touch that makes connoisseurs sigh began, you will notice, as a Suffolk boy drawing his own fields and girls.
subchapters.caption: The Morning Walk (Mr and Mrs William Hallett) — Thomas Gainsborough

subchapters.title: Stubbs — Whistlejacket
subchapters.text: George Stubbs's Whistlejacket, about 1762, stops everyone: a life-size chestnut Arabian stallion rearing against — nothing. No rider, no landscape, no ground shadow, just the horse, nearly three metres of canvas, every vein and flare of nostril observed by the man who had spent years dissecting horses and published The Anatomy of the Horse from his own engravings. The Marquess of Rockingham commissioned portraits of his racehorses; whether this bare ground was the finished intention or a backdrop never added is still debated, and the result feels startlingly modern either way — a Pop image two centuries early. Stubbs painted lions, zebras, a kangaroo from description, and the fallen hunter; but this horse, alone in the void, is his icon.
subchapters.caption: Whistlejacket — George Stubbs

chapters.title: Turner — Light, Steam and the Passing of Sail
chapters.intro: Joseph Mallard William Turner turned landscape into weather, history and autobiography, and he arranged to live here: he bequeathed his work to the nation and stipulated that two of his pictures hang beside Claude forever. These rooms are his arena — a ghost warship, a train in the rain, and Venice dissolving in light.

subchapters.title: The Fighting Temeraire
subchapters.text: Welcome to the painting Britain voted its favourite in a national poll: The Fighting Temeraire of 1839. The Temeraire was a 98-gun warship, second in line at Trafalgar in 1805; by 1838 she was a rotting hulk, and Turner shows her last journey up the Thames to the breaker's yard, towed by a small, black paddle tug. The old ship glows like a ghost in golden light, flags flying, while the tug — steam, soot, the future — does the work. Turner took liberties: her masts had already been removed and the tow ran the other way. He was not painting a news report but an elegy — for sail, and for himself at sixty-four. Everything he knew about light is in that sky.
subchapters.directions: Head to the Turner rooms in the East Wing.
subchapters.caption: The Fighting Temeraire — J.M.W. Turner

subchapters.title: Rain, Steam, and Speed — and the Hare
subchapters.text: Nearby, Rain, Steam, and Speed of 1844 hurtles a Great Western train over Maidenhead bridge through a shimmering downpour, the locomotive a dark projectile trailing fire, the landscape dissolved in rain and speed. Turner, who reportedly stuck his head out of a train window in a storm to feel it, embraces here the very modernity that killed the Temeraire — and finds it just as sublime. Look low at the right for the picture's secret: a tiny hare running ahead of the train, old nature outrunning the machine, just barely, for now. Put the two pictures together and you have Turner's whole philosophy in one room: everything passes, and passing is beautiful.
subchapters.caption: Rain, Steam, and Speed — The Great Western Railway — J.M.W. Turner

subchapters.title: Dido Building Carthage — Beside Claude, as Ordered
subchapters.text: Turner's Dido building Carthage of 1815, his grandest classical landscape, hangs — by his own testamentary instruction — beside Claude Lorrain's Seaport with the Embarkation of the Queen of Sheba. Turner idolised Claude and, in his will, required the pairing as the price of his bequest, so the two pictures have faced the world together ever since, pupil challenging master across one wall. Judge the contest yourself: Claude's light is serener, Turner's more golden and crowded, the rising Carthage all bustle and omen — we know Dido's city, and Dido, are doomed. It is the most touching piece of artistic ambition in the building: Turner did not just want to be collected; he wanted to be measured.
subchapters.caption: Dido Building Carthage — J.M.W. Turner

subchapters.title: Turner's Venice and Late Work
subchapters.text: Turner's Venice, visited in 1819, 1833 and 1840, dissolved in his hands into pure atmosphere — the Doge's Palace and the Grand Canal rendered in washes where architecture is an excuse for dawn. The gallery's Venetian Turners, and seascapes like the Shipwreck and Calais Pier from his storm-obsessed earlier years, chart the loosening of his hand across fifty years. Critics of his lifetime accused the late pictures of being painted with 'soapsuds and whitewash'; Ruskin defended him in Modern Painters, the book that made Victorian art criticism. By his death in 1851 Turner had travelled from topographical draughtsman to something like an abstract painter, and this room lets you walk the whole distance in twenty paces.
subchapters.caption: Calais Pier — J.M.W. Turner

subchapters.title: Joseph Wright and Goya — Light of Other Kinds
subchapters.text: Two neighbours sharpen Turner's context. Joseph Wright of Derby's Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump of 1768 stages Enlightenment science as drama: a lecturer demonstrates a vacuum while a cockatoo struggles in the glass receiver, children flinch, a couple daydream, and the moon — Lunar Society moonlight — shines in the window. It is candlelit philosophy, Derby's answer to history painting. And Francisco Goya's Portrait of the Duke of Wellington, begun 1812, shows the hero of the Peninsular War exhausted, decorations pinned on a face already tired of glory — Spain's greatest painter portraying Britain's, without flattery on either side. Between Wright's lamp and Goya's stare, British and European Romanticism shake hands.
subchapters.caption: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump — Joseph Wright of Derby

chapters.caption: Turner, The Fighting Temeraire (1839) — voted Britain's favourite painting

chapters.title: Constable — One Loved Valley
chapters.intro: John Constable did the opposite of Turner: instead of the world, one valley; instead of dissolving form, grounding it. The Stour valley in Suffolk, where he was born in a mill-owner's family, became his lifelong subject — and, after initial indifference at home, a revelation to France.

subchapters.title: The Hay Wain
subchapters.text: Find The Hay Wain of 1821: a horse-drawn hay cart fording the River Stour beside Flatford Mill, Willy Lott's house at the left, a dog watching, a boatman, harvesters in the distance — and a sky taking up half the canvas, doing most of the talking. Constable called skies 'the chief organ of sentiment' in landscape and studied clouds like a meteorologist, making annotated sky studies that scientists still admire. He built this six-foot canvas in his London studio from outdoor sketches, flicking white highlights on with a palette knife — contemporaries mocked it as 'Constable's snow'. The scene still exists, barely changed, at Flatford: this is reportage raised to poetry.
subchapters.directions: Continue into the British landscape rooms.
subchapters.caption: The Hay Wain — John Constable

subchapters.title: Rejected at Home, Crowned in Paris
subchapters.text: The Hay Wain's history has a delicious irony. Shown at the Royal Academy in 1821, it failed to sell in England — too big, too green, too ordinary a subject for a major canvas. In 1824 it went to the Paris Salon, where French painters and critics went wild: it won a gold medal from Charles X, Delacroix repainted parts of his own Massacre at Chios after seeing its colour, and Constable became a prophet honoured everywhere except, commercially, at home. The French recognised what London missed — that this was a new kind of truth, landscape painted from immersion rather than recipe. Constable, stubborn Suffolk patriot, enjoyed the medals and stayed exactly where he was, painting the Stour.
subchapters.caption: The Massacre at Chios — Eugène Delacroix

subchapters.title: The Cornfield, Salisbury Cathedral and the Six-Footers
subchapters.text: Around the Hay Wain hang its siblings, the 'six-footers' — the great exhibition canvases of the Stour: The White Horse, Stratford Mill, The Leaping Horse with its horse jumping a canal barrier in mid-air. Quieter masterpieces reward a search: The Cornfield of 1826, a lane at East Bergholt with a boy lying to drink from a spring, sheep, and a church tower through the trees — Constable called it 'The Lane', and it was the picture London finally loved in his lifetime. Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds, painted for his friend Bishop Fisher, frames the spire through a dark arch of trees, a rainbow of reassurance after his wife's illness: Constable's skies always carry his feelings, dated like diary entries.
subchapters.caption: The Cornfield — John Constable

subchapters.title: Cloud Studies and Oil Sketches
subchapters.text: If the small oil sketches are on view, stop longest there. Constable's cloud studies of 1821–22, painted at Hampstead, are annotated on the back with date, hour and wind direction — meteorology and painting in one gesture, clouds named almost in Linnaeus's spirit. His full-size oil sketches for the six-footers, once considered mere preparations, are now prized as the freest painting of the age: all the energy, none of the finish. The gallery's collection lets you compare sketch and exhibition canvas side by side and decide which Constable you prefer — the reporter or the poet. Modern taste usually picks the sketches; Constable himself needed the big, finished machines to make his reputation and his living.
subchapters.caption: Cloud Study — John Constable

subchapters.title: Constable and Turner — The Great Rivalry
subchapters.text: Constable and Turner, born a year apart, defined British landscape in opposite ways and knew it. At the Royal Academy exhibition of 1832, Turner, finding his golden seascape hung beside Constable's red-splashed Opening of Waterloo Bridge, stepped in the day before opening, added a single red buoy to his own picture, and walked out — Constable said he had 'been here and fired a gun'. Turner dissolves the world into light; Constable anchors it in one loved valley, every leaf placed. You have now seen both at full strength, in rooms a minute apart, free. The contest has no winner, which is why British landscape painting still lives in the space between them.
subchapters.caption: The Opening of Waterloo Bridge — John Constable

chapters.caption: Constable, The Hay Wain (1821) — England's most famous landscape

chapters.title: Impressionists — Monet, Seurat and the New Painting
chapters.intro: The last rooms jump the Channel and the century. In the 1860s and 70s young Paris painters took painting outdoors, traded bitumen for bright pigment in tubes, and were laughed at for it — 'impressionists', a critic sneered, and they kept the name. The gallery, slow to buy them at the time, now gives them its furthest, fullest rooms.

subchapters.title: Monet — The Water-Lily Pond
subchapters.text: Claude Monet's Water-Lily Pond of 1899 shows the garden he built at Giverny: a Japanese-style bridge arching over a pond he planted with water lilies, weeping willows trailing, the whole scene a shimmer of green reflections with no sky and no horizon. It is one of twelve water-lily pictures painted that summer, the beginning of the obsession that would end, thirty years later, in the great murals of the Orangerie in Paris. Monet bought the land, diverted a stream, hired gardeners, and then painted the result in every light — an artist who constructed his own subject, then let light do the rest. Stand back until the bridge floats free of the foliage; that floating is the point.
subchapters.directions: Head to the Impressionist and Post-Impressionist rooms at the far east end.
subchapters.caption: The Water-Lily Pond — Claude Monet

subchapters.title: Monet in London and the Gare Saint-Lazare
subchapters.text: Monet also painted this city. A refugee from the Franco-Prussian War in 1870–71, he fell for London fog — 'what I love more than anything' — and returned in 1899–1901 to paint the Thames from the Savoy Hotel and St Thomas's Hospital: Waterloo Bridge and Charing Cross dissolving into lavender, gold and grey, the Houses of Parliament a silhouette in coloured mist. The gallery's Thames pictures and its Gare Saint-Lazare, one of his 1877 series of Paris's steam-filled station, pair beautifully: steam and fog, industry and weather, rendered as pure sensation. Monet finished many canvases later in his studio, chasing not a moment but the memory of a hundred moments fused — Impressionism's open secret.
subchapters.caption: The Gare Saint-Lazare — Claude Monet

subchapters.title: Seurat — Bathers at Asnières
subchapters.text: Georges Seurat's Bathers at Asnières, painted in 1883–84 when he was twenty-four, is a huge, calm manifesto: working Parisians and clerks lounging on the bank of the Seine at Asnières, a ferry, a bridge, factory chimneys smoking gently across the river at Clichy. Look closely and the surface is built from distinct, directional touches — the beginnings of the pointillism he would perfect in A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, figures on the opposite bank of which this picture is the deliberate mirror. Rejected by the Salon of 1884, the Bathers helped provoke the independent exhibitions that changed art's institutions forever. Its stillness is radical: modern leisure, painted with the gravity of a Renaissance altarpiece, by a man dead at thirty-one.
subchapters.caption: Bathers at Asnières — Georges Seurat

subchapters.title: Cézanne, Degas and Renoir
subchapters.text: Paul Cézanne, painting in Provence, rebuilt landscape from cylinders and patches of colour — look for his Bathers and the Card Players' grave peasants, and for the Montagne Sainte-Victoire he painted obsessively, trying, he said, to make Impressionism 'solid and durable, like the art of museums'. Edgar Degas preferred rehearsal rooms and racetracks: dancers caught mid-stretch, laundresses, collectors — modern life observed at an angle, cropped like a photograph. Pierre-Auguste Renoir, by contrast, paints pleasure itself, all warmth and dappled skin. The three were shown together, argued constantly, and between them cover modern painting's options: structure, observation, delight. The gallery's holdings let you test each against the others in a single sweep of the eye.
subchapters.caption: The Large Bathers (Les Grandes Baigneuses) — Paul Cézanne

subchapters.title: Pissarro, Sisley and the Boulevard
subchapters.text: Camille Pissarro, the only Impressionist to show in all eight of their exhibitions, became the movement's father figure — and painted London too, lodging in Sydenham and Norwood in 1870–71 and later painting the Boulevard Montmartre in Paris in every season and hour from a hotel window in 1897, a series the gallery samples. Alfred Sisley, English-born and the purest landscapist of the group, painted the Thames at Hampton Court and the flooded Loing with a fidelity his more famous friends sometimes envied. These quieter pictures matter: Impressionism was not three geniuses but a generation, and its average, on a good day in these rooms, was very high indeed.
subchapters.caption: The Boulevard Montmartre at Night — Camille Pissarro

chapters.title: Van Gogh, Gauguin and the Wrap-Up
chapters.intro: The story ends — as the gallery's hang does — in a blaze: two painters who took Impressionism's colour and loaded it with feeling until the paint itself became the subject. Then it is back down the stairs to Trafalgar Square, with a standing invitation: it is all free, and it will all still be here next week.

subchapters.title: Van Gogh — Sunflowers
subchapters.text: The crowds will tell you where the star is: Vincent van Gogh's Sunflowers, painted in Arles in 1888. Van Gogh made a series of sunflower still lifes to decorate the little yellow house he had rented in the south of France, hoping Paul Gauguin would join him and they would found an artists' colony. This version — fifteen flowers in a simple vase against a blazing yellow ground — is the fourth version, and one of the most beloved paintings in the world. Every petal and seed head is built from distinct, directional strokes, so the flowers seem to twist and radiate; and notice the audacity of the scheme, yellow on yellow on yellow, a symphony in one note that never gets monotonous. He signed it simply: Vincent.
subchapters.directions: From the Impressionist rooms, loop back toward the Central Hall.
subchapters.caption: Sunflowers — Vincent van Gogh

subchapters.title: Van Gogh — Van Gogh's Chair and the Long Grass
subchapters.text: Nearby, Van Gogh's Chair of 1888 is the Sunflowers' quiet twin: his own simple rush-seated chair on a tiled floor, pipe and tobacco pouch resting on it, a box of sprouting onions behind — a self-portrait without a person, painted in the same Arles weeks, while its companion picture, Gauguin's armchair, brooded in red and green. Two chairs, two temperaments, one doomed friendship: within weeks of Gauguin's arrival they quarrelled catastrophically, Van Gogh mutilated his own ear, and the colony dream collapsed. Also look for Long Grass with Butterflies and the Courtauld's loans if present — the late, reed-pen energy of a painter who sold almost nothing in his lifetime and died in 1890, aged thirty-seven, unknown. The crowds in this room are his delayed reply.
subchapters.caption: Van Gogh's Chair — Vincent van Gogh

subchapters.title: Gauguin and the Post-Impressionist Break
subchapters.text: Paul Gauguin's pictures here — Breton scenes, the visionary Faa Iheihe from Tahiti, still lifes in homage to Cézanne and Van Gogh — show Post-Impressionism's other road: away from observed light toward symbol, memory and deliberately 'primitive' flatness. Gauguin quarrelled with everyone, sailed for Tahiti in 1891 seeking an unspoiled world his presence helped spoil, and painted some of modern art's most beautiful and most argued-over images. Henri Rousseau, the customs officer who painted jungles he never saw, and Toulouse-Lautrec, chronicler of Montmartre's dance halls, complete the room's argument: after Impressionism, painting could go anywhere — inward, backward, or into dreams. The gallery stops at 1900; Tate Modern, across the river's story, picks up exactly here.
subchapters.caption: Bowl of Fruit and Tankard before a Window — Paul Gauguin

subchapters.title: Van Gogh at Auvers — The Last Weeks
subchapters.text: Van Gogh's final pictures, painted at Auvers-sur-Oise in the seventy days before his death in July 1890, hang in collections across Europe — the gallery's loans and its own late works, like Long Grass with Butterflies, carry that last summer's reed-pen energy: wheatfields, gardens and portraits made at a rate of more than a picture a day. He was thirty-seven, virtually unsold, supported by his brother Theo, who died six months after him. The crowds you navigated to reach the Sunflowers are the delayed reply to that neglect — no painter's posthumous fame has ever grown larger, or been bought at a sadder price. Stand a moment with the late work before the crowds pull you on; it is the sound of a man painting as fast as he could see.
subchapters.caption: Long Grass with Butterflies — Vincent van Gogh

chapters.caption: Van Gogh, Sunflowers (1888) — one of five versions, painted for Gauguin

chapters.title: Wrap-Up — The Route, and Coming Back
chapters.caption: Trafalgar Square from the gallery steps — come back any time, it's free
chapters.intro: Back down the stairs, the square is doing its evening trick of turning gold, and the lions are settling in for the night. One last piece of advice — the best thing about this gallery is that you can come back tomorrow, free, and start again with a single picture.

subchapters.title: The Ones We Walked Past
subchapters.text: As you head back, here's the honest list of what a two-hour route skipped — your reasons to return. Velázquez's Rokeby Venus you met; but there are also whole rooms of French and British portraiture in the Central Hall, Goya's Wellington, Wright's Air Pump, Veronese's ceilings, the Wilton Diptych's companions, and pictures by women artists from Gentileschi to Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun that repay a dedicated visit. Because admission is free, use this place the way Londoners do: in small doses, one wing at a time, twenty minutes with one great painting rather than a footsore march past two hundred. A Friday evening, when the gallery stays open late and the crowds thin, can transform a famous picture you thought you knew.
subchapters.caption: Self-Portrait in a Straw Hat — Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun
